questions.question: What is the difference between `find . -name "*.js" -exec wc -l {} \;` and the same command ending in `{} +`?
options: \; searches recursively while + searches only the current directory
\; runs wc once per file, while + passes many file names to each wc run
+ deletes the files after running wc
There is no difference; + is just shorter syntax
questions.explanation: With \; find starts a new process for every match. With + it batches as many names as fit into each invocation, which is much faster for many files.

questions.question: `find logs -name "*.log" | xargs ls` fails on a file named "app 2026-10-01.log". What is the robust fix?
questions.explanation: xargs splits on whitespace by default. -print0 separates names with NUL bytes, which cannot appear in a path, and xargs -0 splits on them instead.

questions.question: Why is `find . -delete -name "*.log"` dangerous?
options: find evaluates left to right, so -delete runs on every file before -name is checked
-delete ignores the -name test entirely in all positions
-name must always come before the starting directory
It deletes only directories, not files
questions.explanation: find processes its expression left to right. Putting -delete first deletes everything under the starting point. Always put -delete last and dry-run with -print first.

questions.question: What does `find . -name node_modules -prune -o -name "*.js" -print` do?
options: Deletes node_modules and prints the remaining .js files
Prints .js files and the node_modules directory name
Prints .js files while never descending into node_modules directories
questions.explanation: -prune stops find from entering matching directories; -o means otherwise. The explicit -print ensures only the .js matches are printed, not the pruned directory.
